name: How to Read a Savings Claim
title: How to Read a Savings Claim
answer: A verified saving is measured against a clear baseline, over a meaningful period, and includes the costs of the new tool, while a promise is only a projection that has not been tested in the district. Boards need this distinction because promised savings cannot be reinvested in students, but verified savings can. The idea gives boards a set of questions to separate the two before they commit money.

sections.body: Vendors of operations tools often promise dramatic savings, and boards need a way to evaluate those claims rather than accept them. The idea draws a line between a verified saving and a promise: a verified saving is measured against a clear baseline, over a meaningful period, with the costs of the new tool included, while a promise is a projection that has not yet been tested in the district. It solves the problem of boards making budget decisions on assurances instead of data. The questions that separate the two cover what was spent before and how it was measured, what is spent now including license, training, and staff time, and whether other changes such as falling enrollment or new staff could explain the difference. Savings must also be checked for hidden costs that do not appear in the budget.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, the practice is for the board to ask a set of questions about any savings claim and to expect answers backed by data rather than assurances. The questions ask what was spent before and how it was measured, what is spent now including the tool's license, training, and staff time, and whether other changes such as falling enrollment or new staff could explain the difference. Boards should also ask who bears the costs of any savings, because a routing change that saves money but lengthens rides for students with disabilities carries a cost that does not show up in the budget, and an energy change that saves money but makes classrooms too cold carries a cost to learning. A vendor or staff member who cannot answer the questions has not yet shown a verified saving. The text does not give grade bands for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea beyond Figure 19.4, which lists questions boards can ask about any savings claim. It states that the answers should come with data, not assurances, and that a vendor or staff member who cannot answer them has not yet shown a verified saving. It also states that verified savings can be reinvested in students, while promised savings cannot. This idea therefore rests on practice and on the book's own reasoning about how boards should evaluate claims rather than on research evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks in the text are the hidden costs that a savings claim can leave out. A routing change that saves money but lengthens rides for students with disabilities has a cost that does not show up in the budget, and an energy change that saves money but makes classrooms too cold has a cost to learning. Boards should ask who bears the costs of any savings. The decisions stay with the board: it must judge whether a baseline is clear, whether the period is meaningful, whether the new tool's costs are included, and whether other changes explain the difference. A vendor or staff member who cannot answer the questions has not yet shown a verified saving, so the board should not treat the claim as one.
